episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, March 16, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today. 
<break time="0.5s"/>
In Insights & Trends today, at Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are grappling with new challenges in student assessment due to A.I., according to Denver7. Professor Jeff Loats, director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, highlighted the difficulty of validating online assessments. Loats stated, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way."

Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, views this as an opportunity to adjust assessment practices. Meanwhile, Vice Provost Shaun Schafer has adapted his journalism class by switching from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person tasks. This shift aims to incorporate more case studies and community-based assignments that A.I. finds hard to replicate authentically.

Schafer acknowledged the challenges faculty face in altering their teaching methods, noting that faculty buy-in is varied. Some professors allow limited A.I. use, while others restrict it entirely. The diverse approaches across MSU's 100-plus majors reflect the evolving institutional responses to A.I. in education.
<break time="0.75s"/>

Turning to Case Study today, Universidad Austral has partnered with Universidad de La Sabana to implement an A.I. dashboard for student assessment, according to Times Higher Education. This intelligent dashboard allows educators and students to interact with A.I. as both a teammate and a teaching assistant. The tool provides ongoing feedback, helping students develop better judgment in A.I. usage. The collaboration between the two universities highlights the potential for A.I. to enhance educational experiences and outcomes.
<break time="0.75s"/>

Meanwhile, in Practical Tips, the San Diego Community College District is hosting InnovAItion Day on March 20, as reported by City Times. This event will gather faculty, staff, and students to explore responsible A.I. use in education. It features student-led panels and discussions that focus on A.I.'s role in learning. InnovAItion Day aims to foster dialogue and understanding of A.I.'s potential and limitations in the educational sphere.
<break time="0.75s"/>

Over at UNC Greensboro, the School of Nursing is leading A.I. integration efforts, according to UNC Greensboro. The school has appointed A.I. Champions to incorporate artificial intelligence across the curriculum, simulation, and faculty training. Seventy percent of the faculty are actively using A.I. tools to enhance student engagement and accommodate different learning styles. This initiative demonstrates a commitment to leveraging A.I. for improved educational practices in nursing education.
<break time="0.75s"/>

And here's one worth watching in Case Study, Michael Tadesse, a professor at George Washington University, has redesigned his marketing courses to align with the A.I. era, as reported by GW Today. Tadesse's courses now feature an "innovation mindset lab" where students collaborate with real businesses to develop A.I.-enabled prototypes. This approach emphasizes strategic thinking and adaptability over traditional content delivery, preparing students for the evolving demands of the business world.
<break time="0.75s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

topStory.headline: MSU Denver Faculty Say Online Assessments Have Become Impossible to Validate
topStory.summary:
At Metropolitan State University Denver, faculty are confronting challenges with student assessment in the A.I. age, according to Denver7. Jeff Loats, professor and director of the Center for Teaching, Learning and Design at MSU, stated that if assessments are online, "we don't know how to do that in a valid way."

Sam Jay, MSU's Executive Director of Online Learning, described this as an opportunity to "right the ship" on assessment practices. Vice Provost Shaun Schafer described flipping his journalism class from in-person lectures with online assignments to online lectures with in-person assignments. He anticipates more case studies and "apply this to your life, apply to your community" assignments because these are harder for A.I. to complete authentically.

Schafer acknowledged that it is difficult for instructors to drastically change their teaching methods, and faculty buy-in varies. Some professors allow limited A.I. use while others restrict it entirely, creating a patchwork approach. The challenge of creating definitive guidelines across more than 100 majors at MSU illustrates how institutional responses are still evolving.
